newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies-Nov 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST-New Zealand business weeklies-Nov 22.

text.p: Brewer Douglas Myers warned this week that any trade-off in key government policies on tax cuts and public spending limits could destroy the National Party. He said a coalition deal with NZ First that sacrificed core policies would have a long-term political cost, driving National supporters to Act. Myers, Lion Nathan managing director and Business Roundtable chairman, said it was fallacious if National believeeived it could increase public spending without cost to the country. Page 1.

Businessman Selwyn Cushing has been awarded extraordinary costs of $75,000 in his successful defamation action against NZ First leader Winston Peters. The costs far outweigh the $50,000 damages he was awarded by Judge John Dalmer. Peters is to appeal Judge Dalmer's July 3 judgement. Page 1.

State-owned enterprise Trans Power is discussing with its lawyers whether it needs to amend its current bond prospectuses after major customers Contact Energy and ECNZ made good their threats not to pay for the Cook Strait cable. Page 2.

Internet Service provider Voyager is to launch the first of a new range of services which will pose a major threat to the country's major telecommunications carriers' revenues. Voyager is claiming its service, known as Voyager Fax, is unique. It allows people to send faxes on the Internet to 34 centres worldwide at rates 50 percent below current peak rates. Voyager managing director John O'Hara said the company was able to offer the service at such a huge discount because it has spare capacity on its network at a time when other carriers' networks were under peak demand. Page 4.

BellSouth has stepped up its pitch for the increasingly competitive corporate personal communicatons services (PCS) market with three new products. One facility, called Bell-Text, is being described as the "death knell for pagers". Page 4.
The Business Roundtable has called for an end to liquor licensing trusts' monopoly powers, claiming there is no evidence the trusts serve the public better than private enterprise. Page 5.

The Radio Network is certain to dump one of Prospect's brands to introduce its market darling, the ZM format, to the crucial Auckland market. Industry sources are picking Radio Network will sell off floundering Auckkland stations Kool FM, Country FM, Today FM and The Point's FM frequency to satisfy the Commerce Commission demand it divest some key licences after purchasing. Page 12.

Air New Zealand is understood to be close to tying the knot with Singapore Airlines following a four-year courtship of the airline immortalised by its Singapore girls. The tie-up, likely to involve Singapore Airlines buying some, if not all, of Qantas' 19.4 percent Air NZ stake, follows Air NZ's recently-announced deal to buy 50 percent of Australian carrier Ansett Holdings. This new-found access to the Australian market has made the Kiwi airline a much more attractive proposition to the Singaporeans known to have rejected Air NZ's overtures in the past. A survey of gross returns over the past five years shows the sharemarket's riskier second-tier stocks out-performing the blue chips -- by a long shot. The survey conducted this week by The Independent and brokers NZ First Capital showed Christchurch-based medical supplier Ebos, debt collector Baycorp and retailer Hallenstein Glasson have paid their shareholders more than $10 for every dollar invested since 11 January 1991, when the NZSE40 gross index hit its all-time low of 502.24. Of the top 20 performers, only five are included in the NZSE40 index. None would be regarded as "blue-chip". Page 1.

Hetherington Ltd, a substantial shareholder in Asian Properties, this week came a step closer to lodging proceedings in New Zealand against four of its directors. The Court of Appeal has ordered Asian Properties to hand over documents to help Hetherington formulate a proposed claim of breach of fiduciary duty, breach of duty of care and misuse of company assets. Page 1.

Councils in the old Valley Power territory have effectively handed Utilicorp control over their Power New Zealand shares in a shareholding deed agreement signed on Tuesday. The deed redefines the put options and rights of first refusal given Utilicorp by the councils in secret oral agreements from last December. In this latest agreement, Utilicorp agrees to consult the councils -- Matamata-Piako, Thames-Coromandel, Hauraki and South Waikato -- on major or strategic issues. But if, after a maximum of 10 days, agreement cannot be reached, the councils must follow Utilicorp's directive. Page 3.

After nearly a week in the market, the new electricity futures contract is still yet to trade. Launched by the New Zealand Futures and Options Exchange on Monday, the contract attracted bids and offers from electricity companies and major corporate users. But the spreads were wide, and no deals were done. At the NZFOE, business development manager Greg Boland blamed the lack of interest on problems in the underlying electricity market. Page 3.

Environment Minister Simon Upton this week ordered his ministry to produce an urgent report on Auckland's controversial $1.5 billion Britomart project after being asked by Auckland iwi the Ngai Tai ki Tamaki Trust to "call in" the Auckland City Council resource consent applications. Page 5.

Brierley Investments chief executive Paul Collins was confirmed as a director of Australian retailing giant Coles Myer at the company's annual meeting on Tuesday -- an acrimonious six-hour affair punctuated by jeers, booing and a tirade of shareholder abuse aimed largely at director Solomon Lew. Page 7. -- Wellington newsroom (64 4) 473 4746
